entry.title: A draft button that paused, and a shell count that wrapped
entry.summary: Two bugs in Salt Line were reachable from ordinary play. On a controller the third draft card was bound to B, which is also pause, and pause is read first, so the press opened the pause screen and the card was never taken. A very long Standing Orders streak could push the shell reserve past i32::MAX: a debug build panics onto the crash screen and writes no save, and a release build wraps the count negative, which the run reads as out of shells. I fixed both in saltline#167. Grants saturate. The golden-run digest is unchanged, so SIM_EPOCH stays 6.
entry.content:
Two bugs in Salt Line were reachable from ordinary play. On a controller the third draft card was bound to B, which is also pause, and pause is read first, so the press opened the pause screen and the card was never taken. A very long Standing Orders streak could push the shell reserve past i32::MAX: a debug build panics onto the crash screen and writes no save, and a release build wraps the count negative, which the run reads as out of shells. I fixed both in saltline#167. Grants saturate. The golden-run digest is unchanged, so SIM_EPOCH stays 6.

The third card was pause

A draft offers three modifiers. The controller defaults were X, A, and B. Keyboard is 1, 2, and 3, and touch taps the card. Keyboard and touch already took the third card.

B is also pause. Play input asks for pause before it asks for a draft pick, and key and pad presses are taken by the action that asks, so the order is the binding:

/// A run in play: pause, draft picks, then aim, fuse, reposition and fire.
/// Nothing but pause is read while a shot is being replayed or a clear
/// held.
pub(super) fn handle_play_input(&mut self, delta: f64) {
    if self.action_pressed(Action::Back) {
        self.input.touch.cancel_drag();
        self.mode = Mode::Paused;
        return;
    }
    let phase = self.play.run.as_ref().map(|r| r.phase);
    let Some(phase) = phase else { return };

    // A drag only aims on the screen it started on: drafting or a shot in
    // the air forgets it, so it can never drop into a later shot.
    if phase != Phase::Firing || self.play.anim.is_some() || self.play.clear_hold > 0.0 {
        self.input.touch.cancel_drag();
    }

    if phase == Phase::Drafting {
        for (i, action) in [Action::Draft1, Action::Draft2, Action::Draft3]
            .into_iter()
            .enumerate()
        {
            if self.action_pressed(action) {
                let taken = self.play.run.as_mut().and_then(|r| r.take_offer(i));

Draft3 was B, so the press opened pause, the third offer stayed untaken, and the draft stayed open. Y is free while a draft is open. Reposition, replay, and the star read Y on other screens, and the draft branch returns before any of that. The third card is now Y. B still pauses.

The settings screen's DRAFT row lists all three buttons. With a controller in use the prompt is X A Y PICK A MODIFIER.

The test presses B during a draft and checks three things: the mode is paused, the phase is still drafting, and the third offer has no stacks. B again resumes. Y takes that card and leaves the draft.

The reserve stopped at the top of an i32

Shells are an i32. The reserve has no cap unless Forced March imposes one. Taking Forced March drops a reserve of 40 to 15 on the spot. Standing Orders adds the one-shot streak to the shells paid for a clear, and the streak grows by one on every one-shot clear. The grant was a plain add, then the cap:

self.shells = (self.shells + n).min(self.loadout.cap());

Past i32::MAX that panics in debug. A panic is the crash screen, and nothing is written after one, so the run on disk stays as it was. In release the add wraps. A negative reserve is out of shells: shells <= 0 ends the run with RunOver::OutOfShells.

The streak counter had the same shape. It was a u32 incremented with += 1. In debug that panics at u32::MAX. In release it wraps to 0. The bonus was one_shot_streak as i32, and a streak past i32::MAX casts negative in debug and in release.

Grants, the supply screen's +6, and the streak bonus now saturate, and the cap still applies afterwards. With no cap imposed, the cap is i32::MAX.

fn grant(&mut self, n: i32) {
    // An uncapped reserve plus Standing Orders grows without a ceiling.
    // A wrapping add would panic in debug and, in release, turn a huge
    // reserve negative and end the run. Stop at `i32::MAX`, then apply
    // the cap (`i32::MAX` when nothing has imposed one).
    self.shells = self.shells.saturating_add(n).min(self.loadout.cap());
}

if shots <= 1 {
    // Saturating: a streak that has already reached `u32::MAX` must
    // not wrap, and the bonus paid below must not wrap to a negative
    // shell count.
    self.one_shot_streak = self.one_shot_streak.saturating_add(1);
    if self.loadout.standing_orders() {
        let bonus = i32::try_from(self.one_shot_streak).unwrap_or(i32::MAX);
        gain = gain.saturating_add(bonus);
    }
} else {
    self.one_shot_streak = 0;
}
self.grant(gain);

A Depot taken at i32::MAX - 1 stops at i32::MAX. Taking Depot once moves a reserve of 10 to 18, so that grant is 8 shells and the old add would have overflowed. A one-shot clear with Standing Orders and a streak of u32::MAX, starting from 20 shells and no cap, fills the reserve to i32::MAX, leaves the streak at u32::MAX, and the run is still going.

Anything a real run has reached is the same, so the golden-run digest did not move and SIM_EPOCH stays 6.

CI compares the Drone Trial digest on its own

saltline#173 adds a second digest to CI. Drone Trial is on the title, and trial_determinism already replays 200 seeded rounds and prints a digest. CI compared the artillery digest. A replay break that existed only in the trial would still pass the matrix.

The sim job, the Android emulator job, and the iOS simulator job now run that binary beside the artillery one and upload a second file, trial-digest-<platform>.txt, in the same artifact. The determinism job compares the two sets separately. They are different numbers. Each set has to agree with itself: seven copies when the Apple jobs run, and fewer on a gameplay-only pull request, the same count the artillery set already uses.

just android-digest on a phone still runs the artillery binary. The emulator covers the trial on bionic.

I ran cargo run --release -q -p salt-line-sim --bin trial_determinism locally: 200 replays, 139 hits, zero divergences, digest: 0xff8e006571cf0da1, about five seconds. The Android emulator and the iOS simulator steps were left to CI. They spawn the second binary the same way they spawn the artillery digest.

entry.title: I Made My Track Solver a Third Faster Without Changing One Answer
entry.summary: I'm building a racing game in Rust and Godot, a sibling to Salt Line. Every track in it is generated, and every generated track is proven drivable before a player sees it. Proving is slow: a late track costs about four million physics ticks, and a phone does that while the player looks at a menu.
entry.content:
I'm building a racing game in Rust and Godot, a sibling to Salt Line. Every track in it is generated, and every generated track is proven drivable before a player sees it. Proving is slow: a late track costs about four million physics ticks, and a phone does that while the player looks at a menu.

I took 36 percent off the proving time. The solver accepts the same tracks, sets the same timers and reports the same failures as before, bit for bit. Here's how I found the time, and how I know nothing moved.

The Short Version

BeforeAfter
Batch of 54 tracks, one thread9.15 s5.8 s
Mean per track (360 tracks)164 ms106 ms
Slowest track (360 tracks)1,183 ms724 ms
Custom layout proof, median36 ms21 ms
Solver resultsidentical

Those are from a 4-core x86-64 cloud machine, release build. I haven't measured a phone yet.

What "Proven" Costs

A human-like bot drives the track sixteen times to set the checkpoint timer. A perfect bot drives it to find the best possible time, searching which corners to drift. A grip-only bot checks that each drift corner really needs a drift. Then the human-like bot drives it sixteen more times on every car the player could own by that point. A track that fails any of this is redrawn and the whole thing starts again.

The sim is deterministic across Linux, macOS, Windows and phones, and a daily run has to be the same tracks for everyone. So the rule for this work was strict: an optimisation that moves one timer by a quarter second isn't an optimisation. It's a different game.

Save the Answers Before the First Edit

Before I touched anything, I saved the outputs I'd later diff against:

  • the full report of a 40-seed batch: 360 tracks, with every accepted draw, rejection reason and margin
  • the bundled courses, re-proven
  • a survey of custom layouts
  • the cross-platform determinism digest

After every change I ran them again and diffed, ignoring only the timing columns. That turned "I think this is equivalent" into a check that takes seconds.

Where the Time Went

I profiled with callgrind, since perf wasn't available on the machine. The split was nearly even: 52 percent in the perfect bot's drift search, 46 percent in human trials. Per tick, three things stood out:

  • 21 percent building the list of obstacles ahead of the car.
  • 9.5 percent in floor. On x86-64 without SSE4.1, f64::floor is a library call, and finding the road segment under the car made it several times a tick.
  • The human bot's look-ahead took a square root for every segment it could see, about thirty a tick.

Cheaper Ticks

A floor that wasn't needed

The segment index is floor(z / 4), clamped to the track. At or past the first segment boundary, truncating to an integer is the floor. Below it, the answer is zero.

let q = z / SEG_LEN;
if q < 1.0 {
    0
} else {
    (q as u32 as usize).min(self.segments.len() - 1)
}

The cast goes through u32 on purpose. Rust's float-to-integer casts saturate, and the saturating cast to usize is a longer instruction sequence than the one to u32. The clamp to the track length hides the difference.

A test checks the new form against the old one at every segment edge, at NaN, at both infinities and past 2⁶³.

Stop dividing

A track is stored as small integers: milliradians of curve, centimetres of width. That's what makes it identical everywhere and cheap to hash. But the car, the race and the bots were converting those integers to metres on every tick. The track now keeps the converted floats beside the integers. They're the same expressions, computed once, so they're the same bits.

This was the change the profiler undersold. Callgrind counts instructions, and a division is one instruction. The stopwatch said 6 percent.

One square root instead of thirty

The human bot wants the lowest of sqrt(limit² + 2·decel·d) over the road it can see. IEEE-754 square root is exactly rounded, and an exactly rounded function of one variable is monotonic: it can't reorder two values. So the root of the lowest is the lowest root, bit for bit. I take the minimum of the squares and then one root.

Fewer Ticks

Don't choose from one

Before setting the timer, the solver finds the weakest car the track can be met with, by running the perfect bot's full drift search on each. On the first two tracks of a run, and on every custom layout, there is exactly one car. The search ran anyway.

Don't search twice

With several cars, the weakest one's search ran before the track had a timer, and then again after. The bot never reads the timer. So a timer can change a search in only one way: by stopping one of its drives, which then ranks last.

I record how late the search's drives reached each checkpoint. If the calibrated timer would have stopped none of them, a second search would make the same drives and pick the same plan, so I skip it and drive the plan once. If it would have stopped one, I search again as before. A test runs both paths against a full search on generated tracks, with timers from barely enough to generous.

Don't re-plan the plan you have

At each corner the search tries drifting and gripping. The grip branch rebuilt the whole speed profile, which was already the grip profile.

The Bug the Speed-Up Found

One test failed along the way. A layout walled off with rocks must fail to prove, and the test asserts that finding this out cost some ticks. It now reported zero.

A failed calibration had never reported the ticks it spent. The redundant search in front of it had been covering for that. Removing the waste exposed the gap, and I fixed it.

What I Left Alone

After a drift search, the winning plan is driven once more to record its trace. Often that drive repeats the winning branch exactly, and I could prove when. But carrying a trace on every branch of the search costs about what skipping the drive saves.

The sixteen human trials per car are independent, so they'd thread. Track building already runs one proof per core, so I left them alone.

And arm64 has a floor instruction, so the first change will count for less on a phone. The rest doesn't care about the architecture.

What I'd Check in Any Solver

  • Save the outputs you'll diff against before the first edit. If the results are meant to be identical, make that a command, not a belief.
  • Measure instructions and time. The profiler ranked the divisions and the cast low. The stopwatch ranked them high.
  • Prefer changes you can argue for in a sentence. "Square root is monotonic", "truncation is the floor from 1 up" and "the bot never reads the timer" each fit in a code comment, and each is in one.
  • Look for work done to choose between one option. It's easy to write a loop over candidates and never notice the list is usually one long.
  • Treat a test that breaks when you delete waste as a finding. Redundant work hides bugs.

entry.title: trivy-action ignored the severity I set when it uploaded SARIF
entry.summary: The Security tab for cs-server showed about 560 open Trivy alerts, and none of them could be acted on. That count is from the write-up for cs-server#131, as of before the merge.
entry.content:
The Security tab for cs-server showed about 560 open Trivy alerts, and none of them could be acted on. That count is from the write-up for cs-server#131, as of before the merge.

I had already set severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH' on the SARIF step. It was not enough.

There were two causes, both as of that write-up. First, aquasecurity/trivy-action ignores severity for SARIF unless limit-severities-for-sarif is set, so medium, low, and unknown findings were uploaded along with critical and high. Second, every open finding was a Debian CVE with no fixed package yet. About 270 of the alerts, from the same write-up, belong to two categories from earlier job names, .github/workflows/docker.yml:build-and-scan and .github/workflows/nightly.yml:nightly. Nothing uploads to those any more, so they can never close on their own. The pull request does not touch them. Their old analyses have to be deleted by hand.

The current upload category is trivy-${{ matrix.arch }} on the matrix image job. The build-and-scan job still exists. It only aggregates results, and it does not upload SARIF, which is why that old category is stale.

The SARIF step before and after

Before, the SARIF step in .github/workflows/docker.yml and nightly.yml used aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0 with severity and neither of the two options:

- name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
  id: trivy
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0
  with:
    image-ref: ${{ env.LOCAL_IMAGE }}
    format: 'sarif'
    output: 'trivy-results.sarif'
    severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'

After, in cs-server#131 (153b301). nightly.yml mirrors it. The same commit pins trivy-action to the commit behind v0.36.0.

- name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
  id: trivy
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
  with:
    image-ref: ${{ env.LOCAL_IMAGE }}
    format: 'sarif'
    output: 'trivy-results.sarif'
    severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
    # The Security tab gets what can be acted on: critical and high
    # findings that have a fixed package to move to. Without the first
    # option the action ignores `severity` for SARIF and uploads every
    # level. The table below still lists unfixed findings in the log.
    limit-severities-for-sarif: true
    ignore-unfixed: true

- name: Upload Trivy results to GitHub Security
  uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
  if: always() && steps.trivy.outcome == 'success'
  with:
    sarif_file: 'trivy-results.sarif'
    category: trivy-${{ matrix.arch }}

The Security tab should then hold only critical and high findings that have a fix. The table step is unchanged. It still uses format table and severity CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM, so the job log still lists critical, high, and medium findings, fixed or not.

An unfixed critical or high CVE no longer raises an alert and only appears in the job log. When Debian ships a fix, the next scan raises it. If you'd rather see unfixed criticals in the Security tab, drop ignore-unfixed and keep the severity limit.

actionlint passed, and the pull request's own docker.yml run exercised the new options on both architectures.

If you upload Trivy SARIF to code scanning, set limit-severities-for-sarif or severity won't apply. Add ignore-unfixed only if you accept unfixed criticals staying in the log. Leftover analyses under old job-name categories must be deleted by hand.

entry.title: The ReGameDLL nav crash was an uninitialized open-list marker
entry.summary: The SIGSEGV in CNavArea::UpdateOnOpenList() comes from three fields Initialize() never sets. A leftover m_openMarker equal to the live generation makes a new area look open, and the pathfinder follows m_prevOpen. The upstream pull request is still open. My server image rebuilds the library with those fields set.
entry.content:
The SIGSEGV in CNavArea::UpdateOnOpenList() comes from three fields Initialize() never sets. A leftover m_openMarker equal to the live generation makes a new area look open, and the pathfinder follows m_prevOpen. The upstream pull request is still open. My server image rebuilds the library with those fields set.

A crash I've seen three times, and a core dump I didn't expect to have named the function and left the cause open. The bad pointer is in ReGameDLL. This is why.

A new area can already look open

CNavArea::Initialize() sets m_marker and the hash links. It leaves m_nextOpen, m_prevOpen, and m_openMarker untouched. Areas come from new CNavArea, so those three fields keep whatever the allocation held.

IsOpen() is m_openMarker == m_masterMarker. m_masterMarker starts at 1 and counts up by one per search, so early in a server's life the live value is a small integer. Leftover memory holding that same integer is not rare. When it matches, NavAreaBuildPath takes the "already on the open list" branch and UpdateOnOpenList() follows the uninitialized m_prevOpen.

rehlds/ReGameDLL_CS#1202 had the same signature, from hostage path-finding on a server with no bots. It was closed as apparently fixed by later commits. master (1f16a7f) still has this code. That pull request also unlinked areas in the destructor, cleared the open list in DestroyNavigationMap(), and returned immediately from UpdateOnOpenList() when IsOpen() was false. The crash is IsOpen() being true, so that early return never runs for it. The initialization is the fix. rehlds/ReGameDLL_CS#1210 keeps only that.

Set the fields to a value the marker never holds

#1210 is open and unmerged. It writes the three fields in Initialize(), which every constructor calls. 0 is never a live marker: m_masterMarker starts at 1 and MakeNewMarker() skips 0. A new area stays off the list until AddToOpenList().

    // 0 is not a live generation: m_masterMarker starts at 1 and MakeNewMarker() skips 0.
    m_nextOpen = nullptr;
    m_prevOpen = nullptr;
    m_openMarker = 0;

The test NavOpenList::ConstructedAreaIsNotOpen, in regamedll/unittests/nav_openlist_tests.cpp, makes that deterministic. It allocates sizeof(CNavArea), fills the block with the live marker value 1, constructs a CNavArea in that memory, and checks IsOpen() is false. The object is left alive, because ~CNavArea() calls TheCSBots().

TEST(ConstructedAreaIsNotOpen, NavOpenList, 1000)
{
    void *mem = std::malloc(sizeof(CNavArea));
    CHECK("allocation", mem != nullptr);
    if (!mem)
        return;

    unsigned int live = 1;
    auto *bytes = static_cast<unsigned char *>(mem);
    for (size_t i = 0; i + sizeof(live) <= sizeof(CNavArea); i += sizeof(live))
        std::memcpy(bytes + i, &live, sizeof(live));

    CNavArea *area = new (mem) CNavArea();
    CHECK("a new area is not on the open list", !area->IsOpen());
}

I ran the Linux Unittests build the way build.yml does, in debian:11-slim. Without the fix the log is Failure in test 'ConstructedAreaIsNotOpen' : a new area is not on the open list. With the fix it is There were no test failures; Tests executed: 6.

The image rebuilds the library anyway

cs-server#127 (a2b8175) clones tag 5.30.0.814, applies scripts/regamedll-nav-openlist.patch, and installs the rebuilt cs.so over the copy from the release zip. The patch value-initializes the same three fields on the class:

    // Not on the list until AddToOpenList. m_masterMarker starts at 1 and
    // MakeNewMarker() never returns to 0, so 0 is not a live generation.
    // Leaving these uninitialized makes IsOpen() true for leftover heap
    // and UpdateOnOpenList() follows that m_prevOpen (cs-server#122).
    CNavArea *m_nextOpen = nullptr;	// only valid if m_openMarker == m_masterMarker
    CNavArea *m_prevOpen = nullptr;
    unsigned int m_openMarker = 0;

Default member initializers run before the constructor body. Initialize() leaves them as they are, so a new area starts with null links and m_openMarker 0. The Containerfile runs that build at the end of the builder stage. The script and the patch are bind-mounted, so editing the patch re-runs the compile and the copy of /hlds, and the SteamCMD download stays cached:

RUN --mount=type=bind,source=scripts/build-regamedll.sh,target=/usr/local/src/cs-server/build-regamedll.sh \
    --mount=type=bind,source=scripts/regamedll-nav-openlist.patch,target=/usr/local/src/cs-server/regamedll-nav-openlist.patch \
    . /usr/local/share/cs-server/game.env && \
    [ "${GAME_REGAMEDLL}" != 1 ] || bash /usr/local/src/cs-server/build-regamedll.sh \
        "${REGAMEDLL_VERSION}" \
        "/hlds/${GAME}/dlls/cs.so" \
        /usr/local/src/cs-server/regamedll-nav-openlist.patch

Before it compiles, the script requires the patched header to contain the initializer:

grep -q -F 'unsigned int m_openMarker = 0;' \
    "${src}/regamedll/game_shared/bot/nav_area.h" \
    || die "patch did not apply to nav_area.h"

The unit test is the evidence

I have been running 5.30.0.814 rebuilt with this change on a live server since yesterday without problems. That is too short to say anything about a crash this rare. The unit test is the evidence. Upstream master keeps the bug until #1210 merges.

A generation compared for equality is safe when a new object starts at a value the counter can never hold. Fill the allocation with the live marker and construct the object in that memory, and the uninitialized field fails on every run. On the server the same crash showed up three times in a few hundred starts.

entry.title: A GitHub Pages deploy that missed the artifact it just uploaded
entry.summary: The Pages workflow for deathban-pro uploaded the site and then failed. Checkout, staging, and the upload all succeeded. About a second later the deploy step said the artifact wasn't there.
entry.content:
The Pages workflow for deathban-pro uploaded the site and then failed. Checkout, staging, and the upload all succeeded. About a second later the deploy step said the artifact wasn't there.

Run 45110071846 is the deploy of commit c43913e. The upload step finished an artifact named github-pages. The next step, actions/deploy-pages, logged:

Found 0 artifact(s)
Error: No artifacts named "github-pages" were found for this workflow run. Ensure artifacts are uploaded with actions/upload-artifact@v4 or later.

Both steps were in the same job. deploy-pages lists artifacts as soon as it starts, and the upload from that job isn't visible yet. That's the race in actions/deploy-pages#451.

The log says to re-run the deployment. Re-running that run is the wrong recovery. A second upload on the same run then fails, because the run already has an artifact with that name.

Put the deploy in the next job

Upload in a build job. Deploy in a deploy job with needs: build, so it starts only after the upload job has finished. Move the environment block with the deploy step. pages: write and id-token: write stay on the workflow, where they already were.

Before, .github/workflows/pages.yml did the staging, the upload, and the deploy in one job:

jobs:
  deploy:
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Setup Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

      - name: Stage public site
        run: |
          mkdir -p _site
          cp index.html .nojekyll _site/
          if [ -d assets ]; then cp -R assets _site/; fi

      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: '_site'

      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

After, in deathban-pro#82 (69e0bf3):

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Setup Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

      - name: Stage public site
        run: |
          mkdir -p _site
          cp index.html .nojekyll _site/
          if [ -d assets ]; then cp -R assets _site/; fi

      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: '_site'

  # deploy-pages lists artifacts as soon as it starts. In the same job as the
  # upload, that list is often still empty (actions/deploy-pages#451). A later
  # job sees the artifact after the upload job has finished.
  deploy:
    needs: build
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

If a Pages workflow uploads and deploys in one job and then fails with Found 0 artifact(s) right after a successful upload, split it the same way.

entry.title: Running a 32-bit Counter-Strike 1.6 server on Apple silicon (without Rosetta)
entry.summary: I run cs-server, a containerized Counter-Strike 1.6 ScoutzKnivez server on the ReHLDS stack. It lives on a Linux box under Podman and Quadlet. I wanted it to run on a Mac too, with Apple's new container CLI, and the obvious plan was --platform linux/amd64 --rosetta.
entry.content:
I run cs-server, a containerized Counter-Strike 1.6 ScoutzKnivez server on the ReHLDS stack. It lives on a Linux box under Podman and Quadlet. I wanted it to run on a Mac too, with Apple's new container CLI, and the obvious plan was --platform linux/amd64 --rosetta.

That plan failed on the first command.

Rosetta for Linux is x86_64 only

$ container run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --rosetta \
    --entrypoint /hlds/hlds_linux ghcr.io/kevintcoughlin/cs-server -help
Error: failed to exec [/hlds/hlds_linux -help] ... "Exec format error"

The same image's /bin/sh ran fine under Rosetta. The difference is byte 4 of the ELF header:

$ od -An -tx1 -j4 -N1 /hlds/hlds_linux
 01

01 means ELFCLASS32. HLDS, the 2003-era Half-Life Dedicated Server, is a 32-bit i386 binary, and so are its engine, game DLL, Metamod and AMX Mod X modules. Even SteamCMD, which installs the server, is 32-bit. Rosetta for Linux translates 64-bit x86 only. No flag combination changes that.

Tip: before you try any game server on Apple silicon, check the ELF class of its binaries. One od call saves an afternoon.

Plan B: qemu-user inside an arm64 image

Rosetta translates at the CPU level. QEMU's user-mode emulator, qemu-i386, translates a single Linux process instead, so it doesn't care what the host is. The image therefore becomes linux/arm64, ships the i386 libraries through Debian multiarch (libc6:i386 and friends install fine on arm64), and launches the server as qemu-i386 /hlds/hlds_linux ….

Two details kept that small:

  • Copy one binary, not the package. Debian's qemu-user ships every target architecture, about 460 MB. The image copies the static qemu-i386 (14 MB) out of it and purges the package in the same layer.
  • No binfmt registration needed. Apple container has no --privileged. Calling qemu explicitly sidesteps that. hlds_run accepts -binary <path>, so the entrypoint hands it a two-line wrapper.

One trick kept the health check working. The health check looks for a process named hlds_linux in /proc/*/comm. Under qemu, the process name is the emulator's. Running qemu through a symlink named hlds_linux fixes that, because the kernel takes the process name from the path you exec.

Valve's libraries vs. qemu-user

The engine and AMX Mod X ran on the first try. Steam's client library did not:

Fatal error: futex robust_list not initialized by pthreads
qemu: uncaught target signal 11 (Segmentation fault)

qemu-user doesn't implement the set_robust_list / get_robust_list syscalls. steamclient.so checks that the calling thread has a robust futex list and aborts when it can't read one back.

The fix is a ~100-line LD_PRELOAD shim, cross-compiled with gcc-i686-linux-gnu. It intercepts libc's syscall() and answers get_robust_list with an empty, glibc-shaped list head. "Glibc-shaped" mattered: my first version left futex_offset at 0, and the error changed to "robust_list not pthreads-compatible", which at least showed the check was reading my answer. glibc uses offsetof(__lock) - offsetof(__list.__next), which is −20 on i386. With that value the check passes. Under emulation nothing in the kernel walks that list, so this only satisfies the check.

SteamCMD, which runs at build time, needed three more workarounds:

  1. /proc/cpuinfo. SteamCMD exits(1) without an x86 flags line (it wants SSE). Under qemu-user the file still describes the ARM host. The build sandbox won't let you bind-mount over /proc, and unshare is blocked in container build. So the same shim redirects open("/proc/cpuinfo") to a fake x86 one. Include cpu MHz: without it SteamCMD still bails.
  2. STEAM_PLATFORM=linux32. After self-updating, steamcmd.sh notices uname -m is aarch64 and looks for a linuxarm64 build that isn't there.
  3. DEBUGGER=run-i386. steamcmd.sh already launches its binary through $DEBUGGER and keeps its restart-after-update loop. That makes it the perfect hook for an emulator wrapper.

Finally, the server came up "disconnected from Steam3" until the runtime image got ca-certificates. steamclient.so couldn't open TLS without them. (Worth checking on the x86 image too.)

One Containerfile, two architectures

I didn't want a separate Mac Containerfile. Everything architecture-specific lives in one script, i386-compat.sh:

amd64arm64
i386 librarieslib32* biarch packages (unchanged)multiarch :i386 + ca-certificates
Build-time i386 tools (run-i386)exec "$@"qemu-i386 + shim + fake cpuinfo
Server launchernot installedqemu symlink named hlds_linux

The Containerfile calls run-i386 ./amxxpc and DEBUGGER=run-i386 steamcmd.sh. On x86 those are a no-op exec, so the Linux image builds the same way as before (CI agrees). One gotcha: Apple's builder doesn't set TARGETARCH, so FROM stage-${TARGETARCH} fails with invalid ref: stage-. Branch inside a script instead.

Does it hold up?

On an M-series Mac with 2 vCPUs, 20 slots and 10 bots, at sys_ticrate 1000 with pingboost 2:

  • ~250 server FPS, which is plenty for LAN and friends (clients update at ≤100 Hz)
  • ~50–80% of the VM's CPU and ~340 MiB of RAM
  • the server connects to Steam in secure mode, and answers A2S queries on the LAN
  • a from-source image build in about ten minutes, most of it SteamCMD downloading under emulation

For a busy public server I'd still use Linux on x86. For a Mac in the living room on LAN night, it's more than enough. A small launchd agent makes it start at login and restart on crashes, and the in-game shutdown countdown still runs on stop.

Takeaways

  • Check the ELF class first. Rosetta for Linux won't run 32-bit x86.
  • qemu-user is a real option for small, old, single-process servers. Copy just the one target binary into your image.
  • Most breakage was at the edges: syscalls qemu doesn't implement, /proc files describing the wrong CPU, and scripts that sniff uname -m. An LD_PRELOAD shim covers a surprising amount of that.
  • Keep architecture logic in one script with a no-op path for the native case. Then the x86 build doesn't change.

The full change is cs-server#56. The interesting files are scripts/i386-compat.sh and scripts/i386-qemu-shim.c.

entry.title: Small Findings
entry.summary: Short notes from side projects. Each one is something I measured or hit, not a general claim.
entry.content:
Short notes from side projects. Each one is something I measured or hit, not a general claim.

Godot 4.8 beta 2 makes my Android APK about 6 MB smaller

2026-11-02

Salt Line, my Rust + Godot artillery game, ships on Godot 4.7.2. I keep an opt-in CI job that exports the same project with both 4.7.2 and 4.8-beta2 and compares the results.

Both exports below use Godot's official export templates, for arm64 Android, with release builds. My shipping 4.7.2 build uses a stripped custom engine instead, so these aren't my store sizes. They do compare like with like.

4.7.24.8-beta2Change
Salt Line APK90,869,703 B84,594,405 B−6,275,298 B (−6.9%)
libgodot_android.so in the APK71,114,944 B64,818,536 B−6,296,408 B (−8.9%)
libsalt_line_godot.so (my Rust GDExtension) in the APK6,077,720 B6,077,720 B0 B

Almost all of the drop is the engine library. My own native library is byte-for-byte the same size. So the savings come from Godot, not from anything I changed.

Not everything got smaller. The Linux x86_64 release export grew by 3,135,744 B (78.6 MB → 81.7 MB), the same amount as the official Linux template grew. I haven't looked into what changed in the engine on either platform.

The numbers come from one CI run (41565869845) against 4.8-beta2 commit cafc17a19. Betas change, so I'll measure again at the release candidate.

The export that didn't build at first

The first 4.8 Android export failed in Gradle:

GodotApp.java:49: error: cannot find symbol
  symbol:   variable FLAVOR
  location: class BuildConfig

4.8 moved com/godot/game/GodotApp.java to com/godot/game/app/GodotApplication.java. My build script unpacked the 4.8 Android build template over the 4.7.2 one that the job had just used, so the old GodotApp.java stayed behind and was compiled against 4.8's Gradle project.

The fix was to delete android/build before unpacking the template (saltline#144). If you switch Godot versions in one checkout and see a strange Java error in the Android export, check for files left over from the old template.

Godot 4.8: vulkan=false is no longer enough for a Vulkan-less build

2026-11-12

I ship Salt Line with a stripped Godot engine, compiled from a build profile that turns off what the game doesn't use, Vulkan included. On Godot 4.7.2 that profile sets "vulkan": false. When I built the same profile against 4.8-beta3, the Android template stopped compiling:

platform/android/display_server_android.cpp:883:2: error: use of undeclared identifier 'free_vulkan_global_context'

The cause is a new option in 4.8. SConstruct now has a rendering_device option, on by default, and defines RD_ENABLED from it. In 4.7.2, only the Vulkan driver turned on RD_ENABLED on Android. So vulkan=false now leaves RD_ENABLED defined without VULKAN_ENABLED. The Android display server's destructor calls free_vulkan_global_context() under #if defined(RD_ENABLED), but the header only declares that function under #ifdef VULKAN_ENABLED.

The fix is to turn off the new option as well:

"vulkan": false,
"rendering_device": false

That's also the setting you want: with no Vulkan driver there's nothing for RenderingDevice to drive. You can't put it in a profile you still use for 4.7.2, though, because 4.7.2 doesn't have the option. My trial build adds it on top of the 4.7.2 profile and checks that every option it sets exists in the Godot tree it builds (saltline#154).

With that change, the stripped 4.8-beta3 arm64 libgodot_android.so is 21,041,224 B, against 23,186,048 B for my shipping 4.7.2 engine. That's 2.1 MB (9%) smaller, before I've tried turning off the new tilemap and texture_streaming modules.

The same code is on beta2 and on Godot's master, so this isn't a beta3 regression. I only hit it now because beta2's trial never built the stripped engine. If you build a Vulkan-less Godot 4.8, set rendering_device=false too.

A GitHub traffic referrer that was only bots

2026-11-04

GitHub's traffic page started listing aocr.org as a referrer. Every one of my repos spiked on the same day, 2026-10-29. The "visitors" landed on old merged PRs and on .gitignore, which nobody reads on purpose. The site itself sits behind a Cloudflare challenge.

GitHub builds its referrer list from the Referer header, and any client can set that header to anything. This is referrer spam. I'm treating referrer counts as noise until I have install counts to compare against.

My media keys never worked, and I didn't notice

2026-11-04

mediactl in wezterm-media sends media keys on macOS by posting an NSEvent from otherEventWithType:14 subtype:8. It used key codes 1016, 1017 and 1018 for play, next and previous. But NX_KEYTYPE_PLAY, NX_KEYTYPE_NEXT and NX_KEYTYPE_PREVIOUS in IOKit/hidsystem/ev_keymap.h are 16, 17 and 18. So those three keys never did anything.

Nobody noticed because my Mac controlled playback through AppleScript instead. The fix is wezterm-media#4.

"STEAM validation rejected" was a text file with the wrong number in it

2026-11-22

cs-server is my containerized Counter-Strike 1.6 server. It had bots, a passing health check, a connection to Steam and VAC turned on. Then I joined it from a real game client for the first time and got STEAM validation rejected.

The image had 70 in steam_appid.txt. That is Half-Life's Steam app id; Counter-Strike's is 10. The engine normally rewrites that file at startup with the id of the game it is running. My container has a read-only root filesystem, so it couldn't, and the server signed on to Steam as Half-Life. Steam then refused every ticket a Counter-Strike client presented. The one hint in the log was a line I had read past many times:

Setting breakpad minidump AppID = 70

I confirmed it by starting the same image with the file set to 10. The same client connected and the server logged STEAM USERID validated.

Nothing automated could have caught this. Bots don't authenticate, and neither do the server-browser query or my health check. The fix writes each game's own id at build time (cs-server#114). If you run a GoldSrc server on a read-only filesystem, check that file.

A config file my server couldn't read, and didn't complain about

2026-11-22

My installer for the same server copies server.cfg into a directory under ~/.config and used to set it to mode 600, because the file can hold an RCON password. A server installed that way ran on stock settings and said nothing about it.

The server process runs as a non-root user inside the container (uid 10001). Under rootless Podman my own user maps to root in the container, so the bind-mounted file showed up as owned by root with mode 600, and the server's user fell under "other". The engine doesn't treat a config file it can't open as an error. It carries on with defaults. The only trace was from a plugin that reads the map cycle:

Couldn't read file "mapcycle.txt"

I found it when I test-installed a second game, Day of Defeat, and its hostname came up as "Half-Life" instead of the one in its config.

The fix was mode 644 for the files inside a directory that stays 700 (cs-server#109). Other users on the host still can't reach the files, because they can't get through the directory. The container can, because each file is mounted on its own and the container never walks the host path.

Tf_sg.sc: a file name that only works on x86

2026-11-22

I added Team Fortress Classic to the same image build. It passed its test on amd64 and died on arm64, where the 32-bit server runs under qemu-i386:

Host_Error: EV_Precache_internal: file events/wpn/tf_sg.sc missing from server

I blamed SteamCMD, which has a known habit of not downloading every file in one pass, and wrote two different retry loops to make the download "complete". Both were wrong. The download had been complete the whole time. The file is there, as Tf_sg.sc with a capital T, and the game asks for tf_sg.sc.

On x86 the engine finds it anyway. Under qemu-i386 on arm64 it doesn't. I haven't worked out why the lookup behaves differently there. The fix doesn't depend on knowing: the build adds a lower-case symlink next to every mixed-case file in the game directory (cs-server#109). Team Fortress Classic had 36 such files; this is the one that stopped the server.

What I'd do differently: list the directory before theorizing about the download.

My CI never ran the Docker release that broke my server

2026-11-22

Docker Engine 29.4.2 (2026-05-01) blocked the socketcall system call in its default seccomp profile, as a mitigation for CVE-2026-31431. 32-bit programs open sockets through that call, so every i386 program lost networking, my game server included. It was reported as moby/moby#52506 and undone five days later in 29.4.3.

I hit it months later on a machine that still had 29.4.2, and worked around it by shipping a copy of Docker's upstream profile and passing it to every docker run. When I went to remove that workaround, I checked what my CI had been testing all along. GitHub's hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners had Docker 28.0.4, which is older than the bug. So CI had never run the broken release, and it couldn't tell me whether a current one worked either.

I removed the copied profile and added a small weekly job that installs the newest Docker Engine on a runner with docker/setup-docker-action and starts the published image under the built-in profile (cs-server#121). Its first run was on 29.10.0 and passed. The installer now refuses 29.4.2 by name.

If your software is sensitive to the container runtime, check which runtime version your CI actually has. Mine was a major version behind the one people install today.

A crash I've seen three times, and a core dump I didn't expect to have

2026-11-22

Two release builds of cs-server in a row failed the same test step: the game server segfaulted on a map change sent a second or two after startup, with bots turned off. The same step passed on every pull request. Locally I got it once in about 350 boots.

The server couldn't write its own crash log, because the container's root filesystem is read-only. But the host is Fedora, and systemd-coredump had kept a record of the crash inside the rootless container:

$ coredumpctl info hlds_linux
  #0  0x00000000f1b4338a n/a (/hlds/cstrike/dlls/cs.so + 0x1fc38a)

The game library is stripped, but it exports its C++ symbols. nm -D on the file puts that address inside CNavArea::UpdateOnOpenList(), which is bot navigation in ReGameDLL. On a server with bots off.

It turned out bots-off wasn't quite off. server.cfg sets bot_quota 10 at every map start, the game adds a bot on the next frame, and my plugin put the quota back to 0 half a second later, kicking it. That half-second bot is the only thing using navigation on such a server. My plugin now hooks the cvar and holds it at 0, so no bot joins (cs-server#124).

I can't say that fixes the crash. At one failure in a few hundred runs, a clean run proves very little, and the faulty pointer is in ReGameDLL's code, not mine. What I can say is that the only suspect is gone, and that coredumpctl is worth checking even when the crash happened in a container.

entry.title: Fixing a Black HDMI Picture on My LG C2 After Installing CleanYourTV
entry.summary: I customized my downstairs LG C2 with CleanYourTV. The next morning, my Apple TV would turn on, but selecting its HDMI input left me staring at a black screen.
entry.content:
I customized my downstairs LG C2 with CleanYourTV. The next morning, my Apple TV would turn on, but selecting its HDMI input left me staring at a black screen.

The TV could see the Apple TV. It could see a video signal. It still wasn't putting that video on the screen.

Here's what I checked over SSH, what restored the picture, and the boot workaround I installed afterward.

Update: The boot workaround has held through a cold boot. I also went back and traced the stale subscription live, and tried to bring back the black screen without the workaround. See Tracing the stale subscription for what that did and didn't prove.

The Setup

  • LG C2, model OLED77C2AUA
  • Firmware 33.31.68
  • webOS SDK 10.3.1
  • CleanYourTV replacing LG's Home launcher
  • Apple TV connected to HDMI 1
  • Existing root SSH access to the TV

These details matter. This is a report from one TV and one firmware combination, not a fix for every LG black screen.

CleanYourTV customizes a rooted webOS TV. Its Home takeover uses writable files and temporary mounts, and on the configuration installed on my TV, it restarts LG's system app manager, SAM. The project's TV changes documentation explains the boot setup. Check your installed scripts too; upstream code can change.

First, Wake the Apple TV

The first SSH check said the Apple TV was connected, but its CEC power state was Off and there was no HDMI signal.

Pressing Home on the Apple TV remote changed that:

{
  "hdmiPlugIn": true,
  "hdmiSignalExist": true,
  "cecPower": "On"
}

So a sleeping Apple TV wasn't the problem, or at least not all of it. The screen was still black.

Check More Than the Selected Input

The following commands run on the TV, after logging in through your existing root SSH connection. The </dev/null redirect keeps luna-send from waiting on SSH's standard input.

# Connected devices and HDMI signal state
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.service.eim/getAllInputStatus '{}' </dev/null

# Which app LG considers foreground
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.applicationManager/getForegroundAppInfo '{}' </dev/null

# Media pipelines and their foreground state
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.media/getActivePipelines '{}' </dev/null

# What is actually connected to the display's video output
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.service.videooutput/getStatus '{}' </dev/null

# Mute state for each media context
luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.service.avmutemanager/getMuteInfo '{}' </dev/null

The results disagreed with each other:

CheckBefore recoveryAfter recovery
Apple TV powerOnOn
HDMI 1 signalPresentPresent
Foreground appcom.webos.app.hdmi1com.webos.app.hdmi1
HDMI media pipelinesNot foregroundForeground
Main video outputDisconnected, no source assignedHDMI 1, 3840 × 2160, 60 Hz, Dolby Vision
HDMI picture muteActiveUnmuted (current context)

The selected input wasn't the whole story. LG's app manager considered HDMI 1 foreground, but the media service still treated its pipelines as background sessions, and the video output had nothing routed to its main display sink.

The Recovery That Worked

I restarted the media service and reopened HDMI 1. Substitute the correct HDMI app if your source uses another port.

systemctl restart umediaserver
sleep 3

luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.applicationManager/closeByAppId \
  '{"id":"com.webos.app.hdmi1"}' </dev/null

sleep 2

luna-send -n 1 -w 5000 \
  luna://com.webos.applicationManager/launch \
  '{"id":"com.webos.app.hdmi1"}' </dev/null

This interrupts media playback. It doesn't reset the TV or erase its settings.

Afterward, the main output was connected to HDMI 1 at 3840 × 2160, 60 Hz, Dolby Vision. The media pipelines became foreground sessions, and the mute manager reported the current session's picture and audio unmuted.

I checked the screen. Apple TV was back.

One diagnostic gotcha: videooutput/getStatus still showed its own muted flag as true. Older media contexts also remained in the mute manager's list. Match mute information to the current output context, and confirm the picture on the TV. One boolean isn't enough.

What Happened

The CleanYourTV boot log (/tmp/cleanyourtv-boot.log, timestamps in seconds since boot) showed:

24.37 home: mounting the launcher over LG's Home, restarting sam
24.67 home: sam restarted
25.68 after-sam: webOS SDK 10.3.1, Home 'com.webos.app.home flutter', services: none

Each process's start time is field 22 of /proc/<pid>/stat, in clock ticks since boot (100 per second here):

cut -d ' ' -f 1,2,22 /proc/$(pidof umediaserver)/stat /proc/$(pidof sam)/stat

2551 (umediaserver) 1022
3940 (sam) 2466

The media service started about 10.2 seconds after boot. SAM's current instance started at 24.66 seconds, matching the restart in the boot log. So the media service was the original process from before the SAM restart, still running more than an hour and a half later when I investigated. Restarting that service and reopening the input repaired the disagreement between app foreground state and media routing.

That matches what I saw: the media service never heard about the SAM restart, and it kept treating HDMI as background even after SAM brought HDMI 1 to the foreground.

Tracing the stale subscription

A week later I went back to find the specific subscription. ls-monitor -s lists every subscription on webOS's Luna bus, and ls-monitor -l maps bus names to processes. Inside umediaserver, a client called com.webos.media.appobserver subscribes to two SAM methods:

com.webos.applicationManager foregroundAppsEx  <- com.webos.media.appobserver  {"extraInfo":true, "subscribe":true}
com.webos.applicationManager getAppLifeStatus  <- com.webos.media.appobserver  {"subscribe":true}

foregroundAppsEx is how the media service learns which app is in the foreground. I briefly turned the workaround off, restarted only SAM, and listed subscriptions again:

com.webos.applicationManager getAppLifeStatus  <- com.webos.media.appobserver  {"subscribe":true}

The app observer re-subscribed to getAppLifeStatus but never to foregroundAppsEx. A minute later it still hadn't. Restarting umediaserver brought both subscriptions back.

That is the stale subscription: after a SAM restart, the media service stops receiving foreground-app updates until it is restarted itself.

Trying to bring the black screen back

Next I tried to recreate the original failure with the workaround off. For each test I checked the media pipelines and the main video output over SSH, and looked at the screen:

TestforegroundAppsExHDMI 1 picture
Restart only SAM, reopen HDMI 1MissingFine
Reboot (same boot order as the incident: media service at 10.3 s, SAM restarted at 33.9 s), switch to HDMI 1MissingFine
From that boot: TV off with the LG remote, wake with the Apple TV remote over CECMissingFine

The stale subscription showed up every time, including on a real boot. The black screen never did. The last test is the closest match to the original morning: the TV sat in standby with a stale media service, and the Apple TV woke it. Standby doesn't restart webOS, so the same umediaserver process carried through.

So here's where it stands:

  • Proven: a SAM restart leaves umediaserver without its foregroundAppsEx subscription, and only restarting umediaserver restores it. Every CleanYourTV boot on this TV restarts SAM.
  • Proven: on the morning of the incident, restarting umediaserver and reopening HDMI 1 fixed a disconnected main output.
  • Not proven: that the missing subscription caused the black screen by itself. In my tests the TV handled HDMI without it, so something else was also involved that morning. A long standby, a particular CEC handshake, or a timing race are all possible, but I couldn't reproduce it on demand.

That also changes how to read the cold-boot result. HDMI came up fine with the workaround, but it came up fine without it too. I'm keeping the workaround anyway. It's cheap, it makes the stale subscription impossible, and it's the same restart that fixed the real failure. I've only seen this on SDK 10.3.1, and it doesn't mean every CleanYourTV installation is affected.

Preparing for the Next Boot

The installed CleanYourTV version already had an after-sam.sh hook. It asks tvprofile.js which running services need restarting after SAM.

On this TV, that decision returned an empty string. I changed the afterSam rule in /media/developer/cleanyourtv/tvprofile.js to return umediaserver for SDK 10.3.1 only:

// before
afterSam: (major > 0 && major < 7) || /\snative$/.test(homeKind) ? 'eim webapp-mgr preload-manager memorymanager' : '',

// after
afterSam: f.sdk === '10.3.1' ? 'umediaserver' : (major > 0 && major < 7) || /\snative$/.test(homeKind) ? 'eim webapp-mgr preload-manager memorymanager' : '',

Other SDK decisions and the existing legacy service rule stay intact. The existing boot hook then restarts the media service before opening Home. This changes a file under /media/developer/cleanyourtv, not the read-only firmware.

I saved the original profile first. Rolling back means restoring that copy; the rollback takes effect on the next boot.

The updated JavaScript passed a syntax check using the TV's own runtime, and the TV returned the expected boot decision.

Since then, the TV has cold-booted with the workaround in place and HDMI came up normally (though, as the tests above show, that alone doesn't prove the workaround is what prevents the failure). Restarting a shared media service can affect other boot media clients, so I kept the workaround specific to the SDK I observed.

A CleanYourTV update can replace the modified profile. After updating, check whether the upstream version addresses the issue before reapplying a local change.

What I'd Check Next Time

  1. Wake the source and verify there is an HDMI signal.
  2. Check the foreground app.
  3. Compare that with the media pipelines and main video output.
  4. If the signal is present but routing is disconnected, restart umediaserver and reopen the input (see above).
  5. Confirm the picture physically before calling it fixed.

I used Codex to collect the SSH diagnostics, work through the recovery, and prepare the local boot workaround. What cracked it was comparing what each service believed: the input was selected; the video just wasn't being routed to the screen.

entry.title: 5x Faster Shell Startup: A macOS Developer Environment Audit
entry.summary: My shell took 2.5 seconds to start. Now it takes 0.47 seconds. Here's what I learned.
entry.content:
My shell took 2.5 seconds to start. Now it takes 0.47 seconds. Here's what I learned.

The Problem

Every new terminal tab felt sluggish. I'd open a tab, wait, then forget what I was about to do. Death by a thousand cuts.

$ time zsh -i -c exit
zsh -i -c exit  0.31s user 0.53s system 33% cpu 2.509 total

2.5 seconds. For a shell prompt.

Finding the Culprits

The usual suspects in a developer's .zshrc:

ToolWhat it doesStartup cost
pyenvPython version manager~300ms
nvsNode version manager~200ms
SDKMANJava/Kotlin version manager~400ms
Google Cloud SDKgcloud CLI~200ms
Oh My ZshShell framework~100ms
Greeting scriptInspirational quotes~500ms

That's 1.7 seconds just from version managers I use maybe once a week.

The Fix: Lazy Loading

The insight: I don't need pyenv initialized until I actually run python. Same for Java, Node, and gcloud.

Before (eager loading)

# Every shell startup pays this cost
eval "$(pyenv init --path)"
eval "$(pyenv init -)"

[[ -s "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh" ]] && source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"

[ -s "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh" ] && . "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh"

After (lazy loading)

# pyenv - only initialize on first use
export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"

_pyenv_init() {
  unfunction pyenv python python3 pip pip3 2>/dev/null
  eval "$(command pyenv init --path)"
  eval "$(command pyenv init -)"
}

pyenv() { _pyenv_init; pyenv "$@" }
python() { _pyenv_init; python "$@" }
python3() { _pyenv_init; python3 "$@" }
pip() { _pyenv_init; pip "$@" }
pip3() { _pyenv_init; pip3 "$@" }

The trick: create shell functions that shadow the real commands. On first invocation, they:

  1. Remove themselves (unfunction)
  2. Initialize the real tool
  3. Forward the call

For nvs and SDKMAN, same pattern:

# Lazy nvs
export NVS_HOME="$HOME/.nvs"
export PATH="$NVS_HOME/default/bin:$PATH"  # Default node available immediately

nvs() {
  unfunction nvs 2>/dev/null
  [ -s "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh" ] && . "$NVS_HOME/nvs.sh"
  nvs "$@"
}

# Lazy SDKMAN
export SDKMAN_DIR="$HOME/.sdkman"

_sdk_init() {
  unfunction sdk java javac gradle kotlin kotlinc 2>/dev/null
  [[ -s "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh" ]] && source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"
}

sdk() { _sdk_init; sdk "$@" }
java() { _sdk_init; java "$@" }
javac() { _sdk_init; javac "$@" }
gradle() { _sdk_init; gradle "$@" }

Key insight for nvs: Add the default node to PATH directly ($NVS_HOME/default/bin). This way node and npm work instantly without loading nvs. Only nvs use triggers full initialization.

Background the greeting

My shell displayed an inspirational quote on startup. Nice, but blocking.

# Before - blocking
[[ -o interactive ]] && ~/.local/bin/greet

# After - non-blocking
[[ -o interactive ]] && { ~/.local/bin/greet & }

The & backgrounds the process. The quote appears after the prompt is ready.

Consolidating Redundant Tools

While auditing, I found duplicate tools:

InstalledAlso installedResolution
tmuxWezterm (has multiplexer)Removed tmux
htopbtopRemoved htop
treeeza --treeRemoved tree
jenvSDKMANRemoved jenv
brew nodenvsRemoved brew node
iTerm2WeztermRemoved iTerm2
BartenderIce (OSS)Removed Bartender

This freed ~440MB and simplified the mental model.

Wezterm vs tmux

Both provide:

  • Split panes
  • Multiple tabs/windows
  • Session persistence
  • Vim-style navigation

Wezterm advantages:

  • GPU-accelerated rendering
  • Lua config (same language as Neovim)
  • Native macOS integration
  • Built-in smart-splits with Neovim

I kept .tmux.conf for SSH into Linux servers, but local development uses Wezterm exclusively.

The Result

$ time zsh -i -c exit
zsh -i -c exit  0.14s user 0.19s system 68% cpu 0.470 total

2.5s → 0.47s (5.3x faster)

First python call adds ~300ms one time. Worth it.

Full .zshrc Structure

# 1. Oh My Zsh (minimal plugins)
plugins=(git)
source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh

# 2. Environment variables (no subshells)
export EDITOR='nvim'
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
# ... other exports

# 3. Lazy-loaded version managers
# pyenv, nvs, sdkman, gcloud (see above)

# 4. Fast tool initialization
eval "$(zoxide init zsh)"    # ~10ms
eval "$(direnv hook zsh)"    # ~10ms
eval "$(starship init zsh)"  # ~20ms

# 5. Aliases and functions
alias ls="eza --icons"
alias cat="bat"
# ...

# 6. Interactive-only (backgrounded)
[[ -o interactive ]] && { ~/.local/bin/greet & }

Takeaways

  1. Measure first: time zsh -i -c exit before optimizing
  2. Lazy load: If you don't use it every session, defer it
  3. Audit dependencies: Version managers accumulate
  4. Consolidate tools: One multiplexer, one file manager, one top replacement
  5. Background nice-to-haves: Quotes, weather, etc.

The best shell is one you don't notice.

Tools mentioned: Wezterm, Starship, eza, bat, zoxide, Ice

entry.title: Network-Aware Minecraft Server on macOS
entry.summary: I wanted my Minecraft server to automatically start when I connect to my home WiFi, gracefully shut down when I leave, and perform daily maintenance restarts like production game servers. Here's how I set it up on macOS.
entry.content:
I wanted my Minecraft server to automatically start when I connect to my home WiFi, gracefully shut down when I leave, and perform daily maintenance restarts like production game servers. Here's how I set it up on macOS.

The Problem

Running a Minecraft server 24/7 on a laptop isn't practical. I wanted it to:

  • Auto-start when connected to my home network ("HomeWiFi")
  • Gracefully save and stop when disconnecting
  • Restart daily with player warnings (like real game servers)
  • Clean up old logs and crash reports automatically
  • Work without manual intervention

The Solution

A shell script (mc-server-manager) with LaunchAgents for network monitoring and scheduled restarts.

WiFi Detection Gotcha

The commonly recommended approach:

networksetup -getairportnetwork en0

Returns "not associated" on 6GHz WiFi networks, even when connected. This is a known bug on newer macOS versions with WiFi 6E.

The fix is to use system_profiler instead:

system_profiler SPAirPortDataType | \
    awk '/Current Network Information:/{getline; gsub(/^[[:space:]]+|:$/,""); print; exit}'

This correctly returns the SSID regardless of which band you're connected to.

Configuration

All settings live in ~/.config/mc-server/config:

# Network
TARGET_SSID="HomeWiFi"

# Server
SERVER_DIR="$HOME/Development/minecraft/minecraft-server/server"
SESSION_NAME="minecraft-server"

# JVM Memory
MIN_RAM="4G"
MAX_RAM="4G"

# Scheduled restart (24h format, local time)
RESTART_ENABLED="true"
RESTART_HOUR="00"
RESTART_MINUTE="00"
RESTART_TIMEZONE="America/Los_Angeles"

# Warning intervals before restart (seconds)
RESTART_WARNINGS="300 60 30 10 5"

JVM Optimization

The script uses modern Aikar's flags optimized for Paper 1.20+ on Java 21:

build_jvm_flags() {
    local flags=(
        "-Xms${MIN_RAM}" "-Xmx${MAX_RAM}"

        # G1GC optimized for Minecraft's allocation patterns
        "-XX:+UseG1GC"
        "-XX:+ParallelRefProcEnabled"
        "-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200"
        "-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions"
        "-XX:+DisableExplicitGC"
        "-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch"

        # G1GC region sizing
        "-XX:G1NewSizePercent=30"
        "-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=40"
        "-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8M"
        "-XX:G1ReservePercent=20"
        "-XX:G1HeapWastePercent=5"
        "-XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget=4"

        # G1GC tuning
        "-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=15"
        "-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=90"
        "-XX:G1RSetUpdatingPauseTimePercent=5"
        "-XX:SurvivorRatio=32"
        "-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=1"
        "-XX:+PerfDisableSharedMem"

        # Debug helpers (no perf impact)
        "-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError"
        "-XX:HeapDumpPath=$DATA_DIR/heapdump.hprof"
    )
    echo "${flags[*]}"
}

Key points:

  • G1GC is ideal for Minecraft's bursty allocation patterns
  • AlwaysPreTouch pre-allocates memory for consistent latency
  • HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError saves a dump for debugging if OOM occurs
  • Match min/max RAM to avoid heap resizing during gameplay

Scheduled Restarts

Like production game servers, the script supports scheduled restarts with player warnings:

restart_server() {
    local reason="${1:-Scheduled maintenance}"

    # Warnings at 5m, 1m, 30s, 10s, 5s
    for secs in 300 60 30 10 5; do
        server_say "[RESTART] Server restarting in $(format_duration $secs) - $reason"
        sleep_until_next_warning
    done

    server_cmd "save-all"
    server_say "[RESTART] Restarting NOW!"
    server_cmd "stop"

    # Wait for graceful shutdown, then cleanup and restart
    cleanup_server
    start_server
}

The cleanup_server function handles maintenance:

  • Removes logs older than 7 days
  • Removes crash reports older than 30 days
  • Clears stale session locks

LaunchAgents

Two LaunchAgents handle automation:

Network Monitor

com.user.minecraft-server-network - Triggers on WiFi changes:

<key>WatchPaths</key>
<array>
    <string>/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences.plist</string>
    <string>/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/NetworkInterfaces.plist</string>
</array>
<key>StartInterval</key>
<integer>60</integer>

Scheduled Restart

com.user.minecraft-server-restart - Daily at midnight:

<key>StartCalendarInterval</key>
<dict>
    <key>Hour</key>
    <integer>0</integer>
    <key>Minute</key>
    <integer>0</integer>
</dict>

Usage

mc-server-manager status    # Show server state, network, config
mc-server-manager start     # Start server
mc-server-manager stop      # Graceful stop with save
mc-server-manager restart   # Full restart with 5m/1m/30s/10s/5s warnings
mc-server-manager quick     # Quick restart (10s warning)
mc-server-manager attach    # Attach to console (Ctrl+B,D to detach)
mc-server-manager config    # Print current config
mc-server-manager cleanup   # Run maintenance manually
mc-server-manager logs      # Tail manager log

Example output from status:

=== Minecraft Server ===
Server running: yes
Network: HomeWiFi (target: HomeWiFi)
Session: minecraft-server
Attach: tmux attach -t minecraft-server

=== Scheduled Restart ===
Enabled: true
Time: 00:00 (America/Los_Angeles)
Warnings: 300 60 30 10 5

=== Config ===
File: ~/.config/mc-server/config
JVM: 4G - 4G

Why tmux over screen?

macOS ships with screen 4.00.03 from 2006. It lacks features like -Logfile and has quirks with detached sessions. tmux is actively maintained, has better scripting support, and integrates well with the rest of my workflow.

Files

FilePurpose
~/.local/bin/mc-server-managerManagement script (v1.1.0)
~/.config/mc-server/configConfiguration
~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-network.plistNetwork monitor
~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-restart.plistScheduled restart
~/.local/share/minecraft-server/manager.logManager logs
~/.local/share/minecraft-server/heapdump.hprofOOM heap dump (if triggered)

Setup

# Load the agents
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-network.plist
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.minecraft-server-restart.plist

# Generate a config file
mc-server-manager config > ~/.config/mc-server/config

# Edit to taste
vim ~/.config/mc-server/config

Now the server manages itself: starts on home WiFi, stops when leaving, restarts nightly with cleanup, and warns players before any restart.
